quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.rationale: This is the primary research objective.

items.link_text: 1850 United States Federal Census - Schuylkill County

entry.rationale: Patrick Flynn's death on 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County is recorded in the tree (F2, cited to S3, a Pennsylvania death certificate). Pennsylvania certificates of that date name the decedent's father and mother, the most direct route to the parents' names. Search Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 (name-searchable) for the certificate, then verify against the image. The tree's ParentChild link to Thomas Flynn (R1) is cited to S1-S3 but rests on no parent-naming record yet, so this certificate is the first test of it.

Ancestry's 1870 United States Federal Census collection (paid, index with image) is the requested source for this item. The tree holds no 1870 record for Patrick, so the item asks whether he sits in a household headed by a Thomas Flynn (tree birth ~1818, Ireland) or by another adult with a shared birthplace. Patrick would be about 25, so a household under a parent or a married household with a parent-generation member both bear on the question. The schedule's birthplace entry tests the Ireland birth in the tree (F1) against the objective's statement that he was born in Pennsylvania. Use the Ancestry index as discovery and check the original image.

The 1860 federal census is name-searchable on FamilySearch. Patrick would be about 15, so a household headed by Thomas Flynn with a son of matching age and Irish birthplace would be direct evidence of the parent-child link the tree asserts (R1, cited to S2, the 1860 census, though no tree fact attaches Patrick to that source). The schedule's relationship-to-head column is what tests the link, so read the image rather than relying on the index alone.

The 1880 federal census is name-searchable on FamilySearch. Thomas Flynn (tree birth ~1818) would be about 62 and Patrick about 35. Whether Thomas is still living, and whether Patrick appears in a household that names a parent or a mother, tests the parentage link and bounds the search for a probate. A Patrick living with a widowed woman of the right age would also raise the mother's name as a lead.

entry.jurisdiction: Pennsylvania (county-level, parish unknown; Schuylkill County and Berks County jurisdictions)
entry.rationale: The parents' marriage is a dedicated item, separate from any child record. The couple's marriage would supply the mother's maiden name only if it was her first marriage, which is not yet known. Search Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 and Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (both name-searchable), then Pennsylvania, Church Marriages, 1682-1976 for a Catholic marriage. Whether the couple married before Patrick's birth (about 1845) corroborates Thomas as a father but does not by itself establish that Patrick is their child. Also check for an earlier marriage of the mother under another surname.

entry.jurisdiction: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (Register of Wills; pre-1811 records under Berks or Northampton)
entry.rationale: Probate filed by the Schuylkill Register of Wills (from 1811) is a primary parentage source when a will or administration names Patrick as a son. Thomas Flynn was born about 1818, so the window runs from Patrick's birth to about age 62, the span set by Thomas's lifespan and not the subject's. The FamilySearch 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' collection is browse-only, so plan an image browse of the docket for the Flynn surname. An estate file naming a mother or siblings also gives the FAN leads.

FAN item. Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017 (name-searchable) can hold deeds in which Thomas Flynn or a Flynn neighbour names family members, adjoining landowners or co-heirs. A deed that names Patrick or a sibling as an heir, or lists the same neighbours as the 1870 and 1880 households, would test the parentage link from a direction the census cannot reach. The window is sized to Thomas's lifespan, as in the probate item.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.informant_bias_notes: For residence facts specifically, the enumerator is a direct witness — they physically visited the dwelling and recorded who lived there. This distinguishes residence from other census facts where the household member is the true informant.

entry.rationale: The 1850 census (already searched for q_002) places Patrick, age 5, in Thomas Flynn's household but states no relationships, so parentage is only inferred from household position. Statewide civil death certificates began in 1906, so this one should exist. Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968, is name-searchable, and the informant often names the decedent's father and mother. Treat any parent names as informant-reported leads, not proof.

A baptism naming Thomas and his wife as parents is the record that places the child with the parents. The tree gives Patrick's birth as Ireland (census and tree) while the objective says Pennsylvania, so the birthplace is unresolved and a Pennsylvania christening may not exist. Search Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (name-searchable) and the Schuylkill County church records collection (name-searchable) for a Patrick Flynn christening, and for christenings of Thomas Flynn's other children whose sponsors may be family (FAN). A dedicated search for Thomas Flynn's marriage to his wife, dated before Patrick's birth around 1845. It supplies the mother's maiden name only if this was her first marriage, and by its date it corroborates Thomas as father. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Search Church Marriages, 1682-1976, and Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900 (both name-searchable). A marriage in Ireland would not appear here, so the absence of a hit is not negative evidence.

Companion test for remarriage. Any later marriage of Thomas, or of his widow, may show a different surname for her, so the surname on the 1835-1846 marriage cannot be assumed to be her birth name. Search Civil Marriages, 1677-1950, and County Marriages, 1775-1991 (both name-searchable) for every marriage of Thomas Flynn, and for a remarriage of a Mrs. Flynn with a child named Patrick. Plan the household searches on the surname the marriage record gives, and treat it as a prior married name until a record confirms her birth name.

The 1870 census, a further household check on whether Patrick and the mother still live with Thomas, and whether the household's relationships match the 1860 entry. Name-searchable on FamilySearch. Its ages and birthplaces are reported by a household member and should be compared with the earlier entries.

Thomas Flynn was born about 1818 and died at an unknown date, so the probate window is sized to his lifespan (his possible death from 1846 to about 1890), not to Patrick's life. A will or administration would name heirs, possibly including Patrick and the widow. The Pennsylvania probate collection is browse-only in the county Register of Wills records, so this is an image browse of the dockets, not a name search.

Thomas Flynn's death or burial record may give his age, parish and family members. Search Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999, and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 (both name-searchable). Thomas's death date is unknown, so the window covers his possible death years.

If Thomas Flynn was naturalized, his declaration or petition often gives his birthplace and may name his wife and children. Search Pennsylvania, Eastern District Naturalization Records, 1795-1952 (name-searchable) for Thomas Flynn. The Irish origin of the family is a lead to test, not established fact.

Friends-and-neighbours (FAN) item. The Pennsylvania Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880 (name-searchable), list deaths in the year before each census. A death in the Flynn household, such as a mother or a sibling, would show a missing family member and give a date to test against the baptism and marriage. Also check other Flynn households listed in Schuylkill for a widow or sister who may be the mother.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Already searched (log_001): the 1850 United States census, name-searchable, placed Patrick Flynn, age 5, in the household of Thomas Flynn (head) at dwelling 84. This shows co-residence only; the 1850 schedule does not state relationships, so the child link stays inferred until a later record states it. Schuylkill County was formed in 1811, so no successor-jurisdiction split applies to this window.

Already searched (log_002): the Ancestry index of the same 1850 census (name-searchable) confirmed the Patrick Flynn entry in the Thomas Flynn household. It is a derivative transcription and adds no independent parentage evidence; it corroborates item 1.

Already searched (log_003): MyHeritage returned no match for Patrick Flynn in the 1850 Schuylkill or wider Pennsylvania search. Negative result; the site may lack this collection, so it does not weaken item 1.

Dependency step: the full 1850 household of Thomas Flynn at dwelling 84 has not been transcribed beyond Patrick (the log records only his entry). Read every member of that household from the image to get the wife's first name and any other children. That name is the identifier the parents' marriage search (item 7) depends on, so this must run first. The 1850 schedule is a name-searchable collection; read the household page as an image if the index omits members.

Subject's own death entry. The tree cites a Pennsylvania death certificate (source S3) for Patrick's death on 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County, but no parent names are recorded from it. Statewide civil death registration was in force by 1908, so the certificate should exist; it ordinarily asks for the decedent's father's and mother's names and birthplaces, which is direct parentage evidence. Find it in the name-searchable Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 collection on FamilySearch, then confirm on the certificate image at the state archives. Also check the Schuylkill newspaper for a 1908 obituary naming surviving siblings.

Tree cites the 1860 federal census (source S2) for this family but no entry from it is recorded and it has not been searched in the log. The 1860 schedule, name-searchable as United States Census 1860, states each member's relationship to the head, so it can test whether Patrick (age about 15) is Thomas's son and name the wife and siblings. Schuylkill County formed 1811; no boundary change applies.

Parentage item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other, distinct from any item on Patrick's own marriage. Search Thomas Flynn as groom, using the wife's first name from item 4, in the name-searchable Pennsylvania County Marriages and Church Marriages collections. A marriage supplies the mother's maiden name only if it was her first; if a second marriage is found or suspected, search her earlier marriages too. The marriage may have taken place in Ireland before emigration (Thomas was born about 1818 in Ireland per the tree); if no Pennsylvania entry turns up, the origin-country item is needed and requires a locality survey first.

Records that place children with the parents. Search the name-searchable Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection for Flynn children baptized in Schuylkill County parishes whose entries name Thomas Flynn as father and the wife as mother. Siblings of Patrick would share the parents and sometimes name them directly; a Patrick Flynn baptism here would be a candidate for the subject's own entry. The locality guide does not give the register start dates for Schuylkill Catholic parishes; check each parish before concluding a record is absent. Sacramental registers are held by the parish or diocese, not the county, so this item may need the parish page on FamilySearch or the diocesan archive.

FAN item required for a parentage question. Read the households at dwellings adjacent to Thomas Flynn's (dwelling 84) in the 1850 schedule, looking for other Flynn households and Irish-born families. A Flynn household next door may be a brother of Thomas or a relative of the wife, and a shared birthplace or shared Irish county would point to where the family came from. This is image browse of the page sequence, not a name search.

Subject's own marriage, to find his wife and, where the entry or its bond names them, his parents or witnesses. Patrick was born about 1845, so a first marriage after the Civil War is likely. Search the name-searchable Pennsylvania County Marriages collection for Patrick Flynn as groom. The witnesses and bondsmen named on the entry are FAN leads; a bride's family member may also supply a parent's name.

Thomas Flynn's estate, if he died in Schuylkill County. Thomas was born about 1818, so his death could fall from the 1850s to about 1900; the window follows his lifespan, not Patrick's. The Schuylkill Register of Wills holds probate from 1811. The FamilySearch Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only, so plan an image browse of the county index; the name-searchable Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds collection is the first check. A will or administration naming Patrick as a son is direct parentage evidence and lists heirs who are FAN leads.

Fallback for the 1908 death certificate (item 5) if the certificate cannot be found or its parent fields are blank. Search the name-searchable Pennsylvania Cemetery Records collection for Thomas Flynn, the wife, and Patrick, since burial entries and monument inscriptions often name the parents or the family plot. The 1850-1880 mortality schedule for Schuylkill County can also be checked here for a Thomas or wife death in that span.

dimensions.rationale: The plan is largely correct and well-grounded in the tree and log data. However, there is one notable gap: the per-test context requires at least one item targeting a post-1850 census (1870, 1880, or 1900) to track Patrick into adulthood, with the 1880 census relationship column being the best direct parentage indicator. items.rationale: Primary research objective. The tree holds the couple and five children; no records have been searched yet for any others.

entry.rationale: Thomas and Sarah Hale's household in 1840. Mary was born about 1836, so a child born about 1830-1835 would appear here aged 5-10. loc_001 lists United States, Census, 1840 as name-searchable. The 1840 schedule gives ages only, so children are counted by age, not name.
First census naming every household member, so any child born up to 1850 who is not yet in the tree should appear with Thomas and Sarah. loc_001 lists United States Census, 1850 as name-searchable.
The 1860 household may still hold children born 1845-1858 and may show a child missed in 1850. loc_001 lists United States Census, 1860 as name-searchable.
The tree records Thomas's death in 1868, so the 1870 household should show Sarah as a widow with any younger children still at home. loc_001 lists United States, Census, 1870 as name-searchable.
Sarah may still be living in 1880, and a household listing may name a child not otherwise recorded. loc_001 lists United States, Census, 1880 as name-searchable.

A child who died young would be absent from the census households. The mortality schedule, a name-searchable national collection, lists deaths in the year before each census and can name a child who never appears in a household.

The Thomas and Sarah Hale marriage bounds the earliest possible birth and may give Sarah's maiden name. Ohio, County Marriages is name-searchable and covers Greene County. If the marriage took place in Pennsylvania, Thomas's birthplace, this search will miss it.

Baptism records for Hale children in Greene County name the parents. Ohio, Church and Civil Births and Baptisms is name-searchable and Ohio, Church Records is name-searchable. These can show children born before the 1841 start of county birth registration.

Ohio, County Births is name-searchable. County birth registration from 1841 can record births of children born after 1847 and name both parents. Coverage before 1867 is partial, so this is a supplement to the baptism search.

Thomas died in 1868, so his estate file would name his heirs. The window is sized to the estate's probate life after his death. Ohio, Probate Records is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Greene County Probate Court dockets. loc_001 notes that probate moved from the Court of Common Pleas to the Probate Court in 1852, so the 1868 file sits with the Probate Court.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

1. pli_001, vital record, East Feliciana Parish marriage register 1824-1835, FamilySearch, name-searchable. Primary.

6. pli_006, other, parish marriage bonds or licences at the East and West Feliciana clerk of court, county_courthouse. Bondsmen are often the bride's father or brother. This is a finding-aid check, since no indexed collection was found.
7. pli_007, other, Louisiana Wills and Deeds 1700-2017, FamilySearch, name-searchable. Contextual check for a marriage settlement or deed of gift.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: The 1880 census is the first federal census to record each person's relationship to the head of household. Patrick (about 35) listed as son of Thomas Flynn (about 62) would be the first direct statement of parentage; the 1850 and 1860 entries only infer it from household position (ps_001). Collection: United States, Census, 1880 (name-searchable).

Closes the 1870 gap named in ps_001. Patrick (about 25) should appear with Thomas Flynn. Also re-read the 1850 and 1860 household images (log_001, log_004) for the wife's given name and the other children, which no assertion yet records; her name is the lead to the mother's identity. Collection: United States, Census, 1870 (name-searchable).

Closes the 1900 gap named in ps_001. Patrick's own household (he died 1908) gives his birth month and year and his parents' birthplaces, which bear on the Ireland versus Pennsylvania birthplace conflict. Collection: United States, Census, 1900 (name-searchable).

Thomas Flynn (born about 1818) may have died between the 1860 census and the 1900 census. His death or burial entry may name his wife and his own parents, and it would date his death for the probate search. Collections: Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 and Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 (both name-searchable). The window is sized to Thomas's own lifespan.

The federal mortality schedules list deaths in the year before each census. A Thomas Flynn death in Schuylkill County in that span would give a death year to anchor the probate search and may name his age and birthplace. Collection: United States Census (Mortality Schedule), 1850-1880 (name-searchable).

The Register of Wills of Schuylkill County holds probate from 1811. A will or administration of Thomas Flynn would name his widow and heirs, which can name Patrick as a son (the direct evidence ps_001 says would advance the conclusion to Proved). The window runs from Patrick's birth to about 60 years after it, since Thomas could die at any point in that span. Collection: Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (browse-only), so this is an image browse of the dockets.

Fallback for the browse-only probate item if its image browse underdelivers. A name search of Thomas Flynn's estate papers in Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017 (name-searchable) may turn up the same will or administration.

Dedicated search for the parents' marriage, separate from the child's own records. It confirms the couple as a unit, gives the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage, and dates the union against Patrick's birth (about 1845). Caveat: the couple may have married in Ireland before emigrating, in which case no Pennsylvania marriage exists and this item returns nothing. Collections: Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991; Pennsylvania, Church Marriages, 1682-1976 (both name-searchable). The marriage alone does not prove parentage.

Remarriage check. If Thomas's widow remarried, or Thomas remarried, a later marriage record for a Flynn in Schuylkill County may give a different surname for the mother. Her earlier marriage (the item above) must not be treated as the only one until this is searched. Collection: Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 (name-searchable).

Baptisms of Patrick's siblings in Schuylkill parishes name both parents. Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese (Diocese of Philadelphia for Schuylkill), not the county, so the indexed Pennsylvania births and christenings collection is the first route and the parish register the fallback. Collection: Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (name-searchable). Window covers children born to Thomas and a wife married about 1840.

Patrick's own marriage. Patrick's baptism likely falls in Ireland, before any Pennsylvania register, so his marriage entry is the likeliest Pennsylvania record to name his parents or his birthplace. Collections: Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 and Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (both name-searchable).

Associates and kin (FAN). Search for other Flynn households in Schuylkill County with Irish-born heads near Thomas's household, such as a brother of Thomas or a nephew, whose records could name the same parents. Also browse the dwellings next to Thomas's in the 1850 (dwelling 84) and 1860 (dwelling 112) images. Collections: United States, Census, 1850 and United States, Census, 1860 (name-searchable), plus image browse of the neighbouring dwellings.

Its earlier plan, pl_002, is completed, and the proof summary ps_001 is still only Probable, so I wrote a new active plan, pl_003, with 13 items (pli_006 to pli_017) in one batch. Nothing else was changed.

Survey of what the tree and log already hold:
- Patrick Flynn (I1) is the subject, with a birth of about 1845 in Ireland and a death on 12 March 1908 in Schuylkill County. Thomas Flynn (I2) is recorded as his father, born about 1818 in Ireland.
- Log entries show Patrick listed in Thomas Flynn's household in the 1850 census (dwelling 84) and the 1860 census (dwelling 112), both name-searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Neither census states relationships.
- The 1908 death certificate names Thomas Flynn as father, but the informant is a son-in-law and the birthplace on it (Pennsylvania) conflicts with the census (Ireland).
- No wife of Thomas is named anywhere in the tree or assertions, so the mother is unidentified.

Plan items in execution order:
1. pli_006, 1880 census, Schuylkill, FamilySearch: the first census with a relationship column.
2. pli_007, 1870 census, Schuylkill, FamilySearch: closes the 1870 gap; also re-reads the 1850 and 1860 households for the wife's name.
3. pli_008, 1900 census, Schuylkill, FamilySearch: closes the 1900 gap.
4. pli_009, death or burial of Thomas Flynn, 1850–1905, FamilySearch.
5. pli_010, federal mortality schedules 1850–1880, FamilySearch.
6. pli_011, Thomas Flynn's probate at the Schuylkill Register of Wills, 1845–1905, county courthouse; browse-only image search.
7. pli_012, fallback for pli_011: name search of Pennsylvania Wills and Deeds on FamilySearch.
8. pli_013, parents' marriage, 1835–1846, Schuylkill, FamilySearch; may have taken place in Ireland.
9. pli_014, remarriage search for the widow or for Thomas, 1846–1905, FamilySearch.
10. pli_015, baptisms of siblings in Schuylkill parishes, 1837–1866, FamilySearch; the register itself is held by the parish or diocese.
11. pli_016, Patrick's own marriage, 1865–1885, Schuylkill, FamilySearch.
12. pli_017, associates (FAN): other Flynn households with Irish-born heads near Thomas's, 1850–1870, plus neighbouring dwellings in the 1850 and 1860 images.

Two notes for the caller. There is no locality entry for Ireland, so no Irish baptism items were planned, and an Irish survey would be needed before planning them. The subject's own FamilySearch hints were not reviewed as a first item, because the tree has no ark for Patrick.

---
This is the new research plan for the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were. It will look through the census years the earlier plan left out (1870, 1880 and 1900), where the 1880 census is the first to state each person's relationship to the head of the household. It will also search for Thomas Flynn's death and his probate papers, for the marriage of Patrick's parents, for baptisms of his brothers and sisters, and for other Flynn households nearby.
Next, the searches begin with the 1880 census, and each result will be logged against its item.

items.rationale: The 1880 census is the first federal census to record each person's relationship to the head of household. Patrick (about 35) listed as son of Thomas Flynn (about 62) would be the first direct statement of parentage; the 1850 and 1860 entries only infer it from household position (ps_001). Collection: United States, Census, 1880 (name-searchable).

Closes the 1870 gap named in ps_001. Patrick (about 25) should appear with Thomas Flynn. Also re-read the 1850 and 1860 household images (log_001, log_004) for the wife's given name and the other children, which no assertion yet records; her name is the lead to the mother's identity. Collection: United States, Census, 1870 (name-searchable).

Closes the 1900 gap named in ps_001. Patrick's own household (he died 1908) gives his birth month and year and his parents' birthplaces, which bear on the Ireland versus Pennsylvania birthplace conflict. Collection: United States, Census, 1900 (name-searchable).

Thomas Flynn (born about 1818) may have died between the 1860 census and the 1900 census. His death or burial entry may name his wife and his own parents, and it would date his death for the probate search. Collections: Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 and Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 (both name-searchable). The window is sized to Thomas's own lifespan.

The federal mortality schedules list deaths in the year before each census. A Thomas Flynn death in Schuylkill County in that span would give a death year to anchor the probate search and may name his age and birthplace. Collection: United States Census (Mortality Schedule), 1850-1880 (name-searchable).

The Register of Wills of Schuylkill County holds probate from 1811. A will or administration of Thomas Flynn would name his widow and heirs, which can name Patrick as a son (the direct evidence ps_001 says would advance the conclusion to Proved). The window runs from Patrick's birth to about 60 years after it, since Thomas could die at any point in that span. Collection: Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (browse-only), so this is an image browse of the dockets.

Fallback for the browse-only probate item if its image browse underdelivers. A name search of Thomas Flynn's estate papers in Pennsylvania, Wills and Deeds, ca. 1700s-2017 (name-searchable) may turn up the same will or administration.

Dedicated search for the parents' marriage, separate from the child's own records. It confirms the couple as a unit, gives the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage, and dates the union against Patrick's birth (about 1845). Caveat: the couple may have married in Ireland before emigrating, in which case no Pennsylvania marriage exists and this item returns nothing. Collections: Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991; Pennsylvania, Church Marriages, 1682-1976 (both name-searchable). The marriage alone does not prove parentage.

Remarriage check. If Thomas's widow remarried, or Thomas remarried, a later marriage record for a Flynn in Schuylkill County may give a different surname for the mother. Her earlier marriage (the item above) must not be treated as the only one until this is searched. Collection: Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 (name-searchable).

Baptisms of Patrick's siblings in Schuylkill parishes name both parents. Catholic sacramental registers are held at the parish or diocese (Diocese of Philadelphia for Schuylkill), not the county, so the indexed Pennsylvania births and christenings collection is the first route and the parish register the fallback. Collection: Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (name-searchable). Window covers children born to Thomas and a wife married about 1840.

Patrick's own marriage. Patrick's baptism likely falls in Ireland, before any Pennsylvania register, so his marriage entry is the likeliest Pennsylvania record to name his parents or his birthplace. Collections: Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 and Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950 (both name-searchable).

Associates and kin (FAN). Search for other Flynn households in Schuylkill County with Irish-born heads near Thomas's household, such as a brother of Thomas or a nephew, whose records could name the same parents. Also browse the dwellings next to Thomas's in the 1850 (dwelling 84) and 1860 (dwelling 112) images. Collections: United States, Census, 1850 and United States, Census, 1860 (name-searchable), plus image browse of the neighbouring dwellings.

items.guide_markdown:
## Württemberg, Germany - 1780-1830

German children baptised with two or more given names were often called by the second in daily life (the wiki's example: Johann Christoph and Johann Friedrich were usually called Christoph and Friedrich) — search later records under the second given name alone as well as the full baptismal name. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Germany_Naming_Customs)

entry.rationale: The subject's baptism (birth 1792, Württemberg) is the most direct source for her parents' names. Search the Germany Births and Baptisms collection (1473000), which locality entry loc_001 covers for this period. Per loc_001's naming quirk, search the full name Anna Margaretha and also Margaretha alone, since German children were often called by a later given name. The surname Bauer is common, so match on the 1792 date and the parents named in the entry, not on the name alone.

Friends, neighbours and associates (FAN) item, required for a parentage question. Once the parish is identified from the sequence 1 item, browse the same parish register for the subject's siblings (their baptisms name the same parents) and for the godparents of the subject's baptism, who are often relatives of the parental family. Search the Germany Births and Baptisms collection (1473000).

The subject's own marriage entry in the Germany Marriages collection (1473009). German marriage entries often state the bride's father's name and home parish, which could name her parents directly. It also gives the surname she used as a bride, which matters if she married more than once.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other, in the Germany Marriages collection (1473009). Its date should fall before the subject's 1792 birth. It corroborates a father found by sequence 1 to 3 and gives the mother's maiden name, if this was her first marriage. Run it once a candidate couple is named. A marriage alone does not prove the subject is their child, so it needs a record placing her with them.

If the father died or the family broke up during the subject's childhood, guardianship (Vormundschaft) or estate records would name the children and their guardian. The window runs from the 1792 birth to about 1830, sized to the father's likely lifespan, not to the subject's own. No collection for this has been confirmed yet, so check the catalogue at execution before searching.

The subject's own death or burial entry, a fallback if no baptism is found. Death entries often state an age and a birthplace, which can point back to the parish and the parents. Searched in the Germany Births and Baptisms and Germany Marriages collections where a burial is indexed, and the Find A Grave cemetery listings.

items.guide_markdown:
## Hamre prestegjeld, Hordaland, Norway - 1765-1800

Norwegian name spellings were set by the recorder and vary between records (the wiki's example: the given name Sivert written as Syver, Sjur, Siver, Sifuer or Siffuer) — search given-name spelling variants, not just the tree's spelling, before concluding a nil. (FamilySearch Wiki: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Norway_Church_Records)

entry.rationale: Direct test of the question. The locality entry loc_001 says Meland, with the farm Hestdal, was a sokn of Hamre prestegjeld and its marriages are in the Hamre church books, so the marriage should appear in the Norway, Marriages, 1660-1926 collection (name-searchable). Search Unna with the patronymic Halsteinsdatter, which records often abbreviate as d. or dtr., and with spelling variants of the given name. The window runs to 1810 because she was born in 1745 and could have married late. The tree holds only her May 1745 birth at Hestdal, with no marriage, spouse or source.

Fallback if the name index in item 1 misses her. Browse the page images of the Hamre marriage register volumes for the same years and read the Meland entries. The volume must be located through the FamilySearch Catalog before browsing, since loc_001 lists only indexed collections; this is a browse-only image search. Recorders spelled names inconsistently, which name indexes often miss.

Identifies the husband from the other side of the union. If Unna married, her children's baptisms in the Hamre registers would name her as mother and the husband as father, so this works even if the marriage entry is lost or missed. Collection: Norway Baptisms, 1634-1927 (name-searchable), with spelling variants of both names.

Spelling-variant check. Run a full-text search on Unna and Halsteinsdatter as separate terms, unscoped across the corpus, via search-full-text. This reaches transcribed page text that name indexes miss when the recorder spelled the names unusually, and it can surface a marriage entry that names her as Halsteinsdatter without a clear index match.

Tests whether she was married by 1801. The census lists the household head and wife, so a married Unna would appear as wife with a named husband. Her marriage may fall after the 1765-1800 locality window, so this sits outside it. Availability of the national census collection is not yet confirmed by a catalog check; confirm before searching.

entry.jurisdiction: Hordaland, Norway (Hamre prestegjeld estate division records)
entry.rationale: FAN item. Her father Halstein's estate division, if one was recorded, would list his heirs by name, including married daughters with their husbands' names. Window sized to the father's likely death, not to the question: a father of a child born 1745 plausibly died between about 1745 and 1800, and the division may be filed years later. Holding institution is the regional state archive for Hordaland; the locality entry does not cover probate.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

A baptism names both parents directly. The FamilySearch profile gives a christening on 14 Mar 1842 at St. Patrick's Church, Pottsville. Search Schuylkill County Church Records (name-searchable) and Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (name-searchable) for that entry and read the parents' names on it. Per the locality guide, Catholic registers are held by the parish or diocese, so the collection copy is the route to the entry. Sibling baptisms at the same church naming Patrick and Mary would test the couple as a unit.

Fallback for the baptism search if the name search finds no entry for Thomas. The Church Records image group for Schuylkill (1842-1895, English and German) is browse-only, so browse it image by image for St. Patrick's baptisms in March 1842 and for entries naming Patrick Kerrigan and Mary Gallagher. The locality guide notes that anthracite-region church films are browse-only.

A census household shows Thomas living with the parents, which places him with them as a child; the 1850 entry is also a source the profile already cites, so verify it directly. Search United States Census 1850 and 1860 (both name-searchable) for Thomas Kerrigan in Pottsville, then read the household for Patrick, Mary and any other Kerrigan members. The 1850 record is the first co-residence test.

A dedicated parents' marriage record. Search Pennsylvania County Marriages, 1775-1991 and Pennsylvania Church Marriages, 1682-1976 (both name-searchable) for Patrick Kerrigan and Mary Gallagher before 1842. The marriage confirms the couple as a unit and gives Mary's maiden name only if it was her first marriage. It may have taken place in Ireland, in which case this search will not find it. The marriage date alone does not prove that Thomas is their child.

Companion test for the maiden name. If Mary was married before Patrick, the Gallagher surname may be a prior married name. Search Pennsylvania County Marriages and Pennsylvania Church Marriages for any Mary Kerrigan or Mary Gallagher marriage in the county, and for a widow Mary Kerrigan remarrying after Patrick's death in 1880. Do not treat a Gallagher match as her birth name until a record confirms it.

Patrick Kerrigan died in Pottsville in 1880 (profile). A probate file or administration would name his children, including Thomas, and could name his widow. The window is sized to Patrick's death year and the years that follow, since estate files are opened after death. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only, and the Schuylkill probate image group (1851-1930) is browse-only; browse the 1880s for Kerrigan.

Burial or death entries for Patrick (died 1880) and Thomas (died 1898) may name a parish, birthplace or parents. Search Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 and Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 (both name-searchable). The state mortality schedule for 1880 (Pennsylvania, Mortality Schedules, 1850-1880, name-searchable) may give Patrick's birthplace. Statewide death registration did not begin until 1906, so these are the main death sources.

FAN-directed check on Patrick's identity. A naturalization declaration for Patrick Kerrigan would confirm his Irish birthplace, which tests the profile's Mayo origin. Schuylkill naturalization records are a browse-only image group (1849-1915). The declaration may also name the country of origin and the date of arrival, which can connect him to the emigrant Kerrigan household.

FAN-directed land check. Deeds from the county Recorder of Deeds (from 1811) may name Patrick Kerrigan, his widow, or their heirs, and a boundary recital names adjoining landowners who are often kin. Schuylkill deed records are a browse-only image group (1815-1900), and much coal-region land was leased from mining companies, so an absence of deeds is expected. Look for a widow's release or heirs' deed naming Thomas.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.
